_about: Events of the FY14 timeline. Each was checked against its sources on the date given.

events.title: Röntgen discovers X-rays
events.text: While experimenting with cathode-ray tubes, Wilhelm Röntgen noticed a new, invisible radiation that could pass through card, wood and even flesh. He sent his report to a scientific society in Würzburg at the end of December. The discovery showed that ordinary matter still hid unknown processes, and it opened the door to the study of the atom and, much later, of the nucleus.

events.title: Becquerel finds radiation from uranium
events.text: Henri Becquerel left uranium salts on photographic plates in a dark drawer on cloudy days. When he developed them, the images were sharp: the uranium sent out radiation without any sunlight. He reported this to the French Academy of Sciences the next day. For the first time, scientists saw that atoms can release energy all by themselves, a clue that a huge store of energy lies inside matter.

events.title: J. J. Thomson and the electron
events.text: At the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, J. J. Thomson argued that cathode rays are made of tiny charged 'corpuscles', far lighter than any atom. We now call them electrons. The atom was no longer the smallest piece of matter. In a fusion plasma, electrons are stripped from the atoms, and controlling this hot mix of electrons and nuclei is the central problem of fusion research.

events.title: The Curies announce radium
events.text: Marie and Pierre Curie searched uranium ore for the source of its strong radiation. In July 1898 they announced polonium, and in December radium, an element far more active than uranium. They called the effect radioactivity. Their careful chemistry showed that the energy came from inside individual atoms, which later helped physicists ask where the Sun's energy comes from.

biography.name: Marie Curie
biography.text: Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, Curie moved to Paris to study physics and chemistry. With her husband Pierre she discovered polonium and radium and helped to create the idea of radioactivity. She shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics and won the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry alone, the first person with prizes in two sciences. Her work proved that atoms hold energy, and she inspired generations of women in science. She died of an illness linked to long radiation exposure.

events.title: Planck's energy quanta
events.text: To explain the light given off by hot objects, Max Planck told the German Physical Society that energy is emitted only in small packets, or quanta. He saw it as a mathematical trick, but it started quantum physics. Without quantum ideas we could not understand how nuclei in the Sun get close enough to fuse, or how hot plasmas radiate away their energy.

biography.name: Max Planck
biography.text: Max Planck was a German theoretical physicist who was born in Kiel and worked for most of his life in Berlin. In 1900 he proposed that energy comes in quanta, an idea he himself found strange. It became the starting point of quantum theory, and he received the Nobel Prize in Physics for 1918. Planck also supported young scientists such as Einstein. In this story he matters because quantum physics explains how fusion is possible at all.

events.title: Einstein's light quanta
events.text: Working as an examiner at the patent office in Bern, Albert Einstein published a paper in Annalen der Physik proposing that light itself travels in quanta. This explained why light knocks electrons out of metals only above a certain frequency. The idea, which later won him the Nobel Prize, showed that energy and matter behave in surprising ways at small scales.

biography.name: Albert Einstein
biography.text: Albert Einstein was born in Ulm, Germany, and did his most famous early work while employed at the Swiss patent office. In 1905 alone he explained the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion and special relativity, which gave us E = mc². He received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics. Later he emigrated to the United States and lived in Princeton. For fusion, his equation is the key: it tells us how much energy is released when mass disappears in a nuclear reaction.

events.title: E = mc²
events.text: In a short follow-up paper, Einstein asked whether a body's inertia depends on its energy content. His answer was yes: mass and energy are equivalent, which we write as E = mc². Because c² is enormous, even a tiny loss of mass releases a great deal of energy. This is the basic reason why fusing light nuclei can power the stars, and perhaps power stations.

events.title: Geiger and Marsden's surprising bounce
events.text: In Manchester, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at thin metal foil under Ernest Rutherford's direction. Most went straight through, but roughly one in eight thousand bounced back. Nobody expected this. The result suggested that something very small and heavy sits inside each atom. It was the first step towards the atomic nucleus, which is where fusion happens.

events.title: Rutherford's nuclear atom
events.text: Ernest Rutherford explained the bouncing alpha particles in a 1911 paper in the Philosophical Magazine. Almost all of an atom's mass, he argued, is packed into a tiny positive nucleus. This model also explains the main obstacle to fusion: two positive nuclei repel each other strongly, so they must move extremely fast, at temperatures of millions of degrees, before they can meet.

biography.name: Ernest Rutherford
biography.text: Ernest Rutherford was born near Nelson, New Zealand, and became the leading experimental physicist of his time in Montreal, Manchester and Cambridge. He named alpha and beta rays, introduced the idea of half-life and won the 1908 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. His team discovered the nucleus, and he later produced the first artificial nuclear reaction. As director of the Cavendish Laboratory he guided Chadwick, Cockcroft, Walton and Oliphant, whose experiments included the first laboratory fusion reactions.

events.title: Bohr's quantum atom
events.text: Niels Bohr, back in Copenhagen after working in Rutherford's laboratory in Manchester, published a new atomic model in July 1913. Electrons move only in certain allowed orbits and give off light when they jump between them. The model explained the spectrum of hydrogen. Today, physicists use these spectral lines to measure what happens inside fusion plasmas, for example how many impurity atoms are present.

biography.name: Niels Bohr
biography.text: Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist from Copenhagen. After working with Rutherford, he built the first quantum model of the atom and won the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics. His institute in Copenhagen, opened in 1921, became a meeting place for the young scientists who created quantum mechanics. In January 1939 he carried the news of nuclear fission to the United States. Bohr connects the quantum revolution with the nuclear age that followed.

events.title: Millikan tests Einstein, and agrees
events.text: Robert Millikan spent about ten years trying to prove Einstein's light-quantum idea wrong. His careful photoelectric measurements, published in 1914 and 1916, matched Einstein's equation and gave an accurate value of Planck's constant. Millikan still doubted the theory for years. The story shows how science works: a bold idea becomes accepted only when careful experiments support it.

events.title: The first artificial nuclear reaction
events.text: Rutherford bombarded nitrogen gas with alpha particles and found that hydrogen nuclei were knocked out. He had changed one element into another, the first nuclear reaction made by humans. In 1920 he named the hydrogen nucleus the proton. The experiment showed that nuclei can be changed on purpose, but only by hitting them very hard.

events.title: Aston's mass spectrograph
events.text: At the Cavendish Laboratory, Francis Aston built a mass spectrograph that could weigh atoms very precisely. He found that isotope masses are nearly whole numbers, but not exactly. By 1920 he had found that a helium atom is slightly lighter than four hydrogen atoms: about 0.8 percent by his measurement (the modern value is 0.7 percent). That small 'missing mass' is the energy source of fusion, as Eddington soon pointed out.

events.title: Eddington: the stars burn hydrogen
events.text: In a lecture to the British Association in Cardiff, Arthur Eddington suggested that stars shine by building helium out of hydrogen, turning the lost mass into energy. He added that this brought humanity closer to the dream of controlling such energy for its own good. It was the first clear statement of the fusion idea, about a century before ITER.

biography.name: Arthur Eddington
biography.text: Arthur Eddington was an English astrophysicist from Kendal who worked at Cambridge. In 1919 he led an eclipse expedition to Príncipe that tested Einstein's theory of gravity. In 1920 he proposed that stars are powered by turning hydrogen into helium, using Aston's mass measurements and E = mc². He also wrote popular books that explained modern physics to the public. In our story he is the person who first said clearly what fusion is and why it might one day be useful.

sources.title: Eddington in Cardiff 100 years ago today (In the Dark blog)

events.title: De Broglie: particles are also waves
events.text: In his doctoral thesis, the French physicist Louis de Broglie proposed that electrons and all other particles also behave like waves. Electron diffraction experiments confirmed it in 1927. This wave nature is important for fusion: because a nucleus is partly a wave, it has a small chance to reach another nucleus even when it does not have enough energy to climb over the repulsion.

events.title: Heisenberg's new mechanics
events.text: While staying on the North Sea island of Heligoland, Werner Heisenberg found a new way to describe atoms using only measurable quantities. Max Born and Pascual Jordan turned his idea into matrix mechanics, the first complete form of quantum mechanics. It led to the uncertainty principle and replaced Bohr's simple orbits with a more powerful theory.

events.title: Schrödinger's wave equation
events.text: Erwin Schrödinger published a wave equation in Annalen der Physik that describes how quantum particles behave. It turned out to be equivalent to Heisenberg's matrix mechanics but was easier for many physicists to use. With it, physicists could calculate how a particle leaks through a barrier, the tunnelling effect that makes fusion in stars possible.

events.title: The Solvay Conference of 1927
events.text: For six days in Brussels, 29 physicists met to discuss 'Electrons and Photons'. Seventeen of them were or later became Nobel laureates, and Einstein and Bohr were the leading voices. The famous group photo shows how international physics had become. Fusion research would later depend on the same kind of open exchange, after years of wartime and Cold War secrecy.

events.title: Gamow explains tunnelling
events.text: Working in Göttingen, the young Soviet physicist George Gamow used quantum mechanics to explain alpha decay. An alpha particle escapes the nucleus by tunnelling through an energy barrier it could not climb classically. The same mathematics works in reverse: incoming nuclei can tunnel inwards. The probability is called the Gamow factor and is used in every fusion rate calculation.

biography.name: George Gamow
biography.text: George Gamow was born in Odessa and studied in Leningrad before working in Göttingen, Copenhagen and Cambridge. In 1928 he explained alpha decay with quantum tunnelling. After failed attempts to escape the Soviet Union, he stayed in the West after the 1933 Solvay Conference and moved to the United States in 1934. He later developed the Big Bang theory and wrote popular science books. His tunnelling idea explains why stars can fuse hydrogen at 'only' millions of degrees.

events.title: Why the stars shine
events.text: Robert Atkinson and Fritz Houtermans used Gamow's tunnelling theory to make the first calculation of fusion reaction rates inside stars. Their paper in Zeitschrift für Physik showed that light nuclei can fuse at stellar temperatures. Houtermans reportedly told a friend that he now knew why the stars shine. The calculation also showed how hard fusion is: even in the Sun, it is a rare event.

events.title: Lawrence's first cyclotron
events.text: At Berkeley, Ernest Lawrence and his student M. Stanley Livingston got a palm-sized cyclotron working, which accelerated protons to 80 keV by spiralling them in a magnetic field. By 1932 a 27-inch machine reached 4.8 MeV. Accelerators let physicists study nuclear reactions in detail, but they also showed that beam fusion wastes far more energy than it produces.

events.title: Chadwick discovers the neutron
events.text: James Chadwick at the Cavendish Laboratory showed that a strange penetrating radiation from beryllium was made of neutral particles about as heavy as protons. He announced the neutron in a letter to Nature in February 1932. Neutrons matter greatly for fusion: most of the energy of deuterium–tritium fusion is carried by fast neutrons, which damage materials and are needed to breed new tritium.

biography.name: James Chadwick
biography.text: James Chadwick was an English physicist who worked with Rutherford in Manchester and Cambridge. In 1932 he discovered the neutron, for which he received the 1935 Nobel Prize in Physics. During the Second World War he led the British mission to the Manhattan Project and worked closely with General Groves. Chadwick matters for fusion because the neutron is both the main energy carrier of deuterium–tritium fusion and one of the biggest engineering problems for future power plants.

events.title: Cockcroft and Walton split lithium
events.text: Ernest Walton and John Cockcroft fired accelerated protons at a lithium target at the Cavendish Laboratory and saw alpha particles come out. It was the first nuclear reaction produced with a particle accelerator, often called 'splitting the atom'. They wrote to Nature the same evening. The experiment showed that light nuclei can be made to react in the laboratory, if they are hit hard enough.

events.title: Rutherford calls atomic power 'moonshine'
events.text: In a September 1933 speech, Rutherford dismissed the idea of getting useful power from atoms as 'moonshine', because accelerator experiments used far more energy than they released. On 12 September Leo Szilard read the report in The Times and imagined a neutron chain reaction. Both men had a point: fission soon became practical, while fusion still struggles to give more energy than it uses.

events.title: First fusion in the laboratory
events.text: Mark Oliphant, Paul Harteck and Rutherford fired deuterium nuclei at targets containing deuterium, using heavy water given to the Cavendish Laboratory. The reactions produced the new isotopes helium-3 and tritium, which was the first artificial fusion. Their paper appeared in May 1934. Tritium, discovered here, is today the main fuel partner of deuterium, but it hardly exists in nature.

events.title: Bethe explains the Sun's energy
events.text: After a conference on stellar energy in Washington, Hans Bethe worked out, partly with Charles Critchfield, how the Sun turns hydrogen into helium step by step: the proton–proton chain. Bethe also found the CNO cycle used by heavier stars, published in Physical Review in 1939. The Sun's slow reactions work only because the Sun is huge; on Earth we need faster fuels and much higher temperatures.

biography.name: Hans Bethe
biography.text: Hans Bethe was born in Strasbourg, then part of Germany, and left Nazi Germany in the 1930s. At Cornell University he explained the nuclear reactions that power the Sun and other stars, and he received the 1967 Nobel Prize in Physics for it. During the war he led the theoretical division at Los Alamos. Later he campaigned for arms control. He links the physics of the stars with the nuclear weapons that kept fusion research secret.

events.title: The discovery of fission
events.text: In Berlin in December 1938, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found barium after bombarding uranium with neutrons. Over Christmas in Sweden, Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained that the uranium nucleus had split in two, releasing about 200 MeV. Fission of heavy nuclei was suddenly a practical energy source. Fusion, the joining of light nuclei, would prove much harder to control.

biography.name: Lise Meitner
biography.text: Lise Meitner was an Austrian physicist from Vienna who worked with Otto Hahn in Berlin for three decades. Because of her Jewish family background she had to flee Nazi Germany in July 1938. From exile in Sweden she and her nephew Otto Frisch gave the physical explanation of fission. The 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Hahn alone, which many now see as unfair. Element 109, meitnerium, is named after her.

events.title: Frisch confirms fission
events.text: Back in Copenhagen, Otto Frisch measured the energetic fragments of split uranium nuclei with a detector. He borrowed the word 'fission' from biology. Bohr took the news to America, and Meitner and Frisch's note appeared in Nature in February 1939. Scientists soon realised that fission also releases extra neutrons, so a chain reaction, and a bomb, might be possible.

events.title: The Einstein–Szilard letter
events.text: In August 1939, Leo Szilard persuaded Albert Einstein to sign a letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt. It warned that uranium chain reactions could make extremely powerful bombs and that Germany might try to build them. The letter helped start American nuclear research. From then on, nuclear physics was closely tied to weapons and to state secrecy.

events.title: The Manhattan Project
events.text: The US Army created the Manhattan District to build an atomic bomb, with General Leslie Groves in charge from September and Robert Oppenheimer leading the Los Alamos laboratory. At its peak it employed nearly 130,000 people and cost about 2 billion dollars. It showed what huge, focused state projects can achieve, and it is often compared, not always fairly, with fusion research budgets.

events.title: Chicago Pile-1 goes critical
events.text: Under the stands of a sports field at the University of Chicago, Enrico Fermi's team achieved the first human-made, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. The pile of graphite and uranium ran for about four and a half minutes at only half a watt. Fission needed four years from discovery to a working reactor; fusion has needed far longer.

events.title: The Trinity test
events.text: Early in the morning in the New Mexico desert, the first nuclear weapon was exploded. Its yield was about 25 kilotons of TNT. Watching scientists understood that the world had changed. Some, like Hans Bethe, would later work on even more powerful fusion weapons, and the link with weapons kept much fusion research secret for more than a decade.

events.title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
events.text: On 6 August 1945 an American atomic bomb destroyed Hiroshima, and on 9 August a second bomb hit Nagasaki. By the end of the year between about 150,000 and 246,000 people had died, most of them civilians. Japan announced its surrender on 15 August. The bombings shaped public fear of anything 'nuclear', including fusion, which works in a very different way.

sources.title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki (Wikipedia)

events.title: The first fusion reactor patent
events.text: At Imperial College London, George Paget Thomson and Moses Blackman filed a provisional patent for a ring-shaped (toroidal) device to confine a hot deuterium plasma with magnetic fields and a current through the plasma. It was the first detailed fusion reactor design. The patent was granted in late 1948, and soon afterwards British fusion work became secret.

events.title: A soldier's fusion letter
events.text: Oleg Lavrentiev, a young Soviet army sergeant on Sakhalin island, wrote to the Communist Party's Central Committee with ideas for an H-bomb and for confining plasma with electric fields. Andrei Sakharov reviewed it and called the problem important and not hopeless. The letter helped push Sakharov and Igor Tamm towards magnetic confinement, the idea behind the tokamak.

biography.name: Andrei Sakharov
biography.text: Andrei Sakharov was a Soviet physicist from Moscow who helped design the first megaton-range Soviet hydrogen bomb, tested in 1955. With Igor Tamm he proposed confining hot plasma in a ring-shaped magnetic field, the idea behind the tokamak. Later he turned against nuclear testing and became a leading human rights campaigner. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1975 and was sent into internal exile in 1980. His life links weapons, peaceful fusion and conscience.

events.title: Tamm and Sakharov's magnetic bottle
events.text: By October 1950, Igor Tamm and Andrei Sakharov had written a proposal to hold hot plasma in a ring-shaped magnetic field, and sent it to Igor Kurchatov. A detailed design followed in 1951, and in May Stalin approved a fusion laboratory led by Lev Artsimovich. This 'magnetic thermonuclear reactor' became the tokamak, the design used in ITER today.

biography.name: Igor Tamm
biography.text: Igor Tamm was a Soviet theoretical physicist born in Vladivostok. From 1949 to 1953 he led a theory group working on the Soviet hydrogen bomb at Sarov, where Andrei Sakharov also worked. With Sakharov he proposed the magnetic confinement scheme that became the tokamak. He shared the 1958 Nobel Prize in Physics for explaining Cherenkov radiation. Tamm shows how weapons scientists became the first designers of peaceful fusion machines.

events.title: Greenhouse George
events.text: In a US weapons test in the Pacific, the heat of a fission explosion was used to make a small amount of fusion fuel react. This was the first artificial thermonuclear fusion on a significant scale. It proved that fusion could be started with enough heat and pressure, but only inside a nuclear explosion, which is useless as a controlled power source.

events.title: Perón's fusion announcement
events.text: At a press conference, Argentine President Juan Perón announced that the scientist Ronald Richter had achieved controlled fusion on Huemul Island. The claim made headlines worldwide. There was no real evidence, but the announcement worried and inspired scientists elsewhere. It was the first of several moments when fusion success was declared far too early.

events.title: Spitzer invents the stellarator
events.text: Princeton astrophysicist Lyman Spitzer read about Richter's claim and doubted it. Thinking about how to confine hot plasma properly, he designed a twisted magnetic bottle, the stellarator. He met the US Atomic Energy Commission in May and received 50,000 dollars. His secret project, Matterhorn, became the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory.

biography.name: Lyman Spitzer
biography.text: Lyman Spitzer was an American astrophysicist from Toledo, Ohio, who worked at Princeton University. In 1951 he invented the stellarator and became the first director of Project Matterhorn, renamed the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory in 1961. He also studied the gas between the stars and was an early champion of telescopes in space, work that led to the Hubble Space Telescope. Spitzer brought an astronomer's view of plasma physics into fusion research.

events.title: Project Sherwood
events.text: The US Atomic Energy Commission gathered its secret fusion efforts into a programme later called Project Sherwood. It included Spitzer's stellarators at Princeton, James Tuck's pinch machine 'Perhapsatron' at Los Alamos and Richard Post's magnetic mirrors at Livermore. Several competing ideas were tried at once, because nobody knew which magnetic bottle would hold a plasma best.

events.title: The Huemul claim collapses
events.text: Argentine physicists led by José Balseiro inspected Richter's laboratory on Huemul Island between 5 and 8 September 1952. They found no sign of fusion, and their reports were published that month. In November the site was occupied and the project was declared a fraud. The affair is an early lesson: in fusion, extraordinary claims need independent measurement.

events.title: Ivy Mike, the first hydrogen bomb
events.text: On Elugelab island in Enewetak Atoll, the United States tested a two-stage thermonuclear device. It released 10.4 megatons and left a crater nearly two kilometres wide. The device weighed 74 tonnes, mostly cooling equipment for liquid deuterium. Ivy Mike showed that large-scale fusion was possible, but only as an uncontrolled explosion, very different from a steady power plant.

events.title: Model A, the first stellarator
events.text: In early 1953, Spitzer's team at Princeton began operating Model A, a small stellarator. It could make plasma but was far too small and cool to produce fusion. Model A started a long series of Princeton machines. Early devices like this soon showed that plasma escapes from magnetic fields much faster than simple theory predicted.

events.title: The Lawson criterion
events.text: At Harwell, engineer John Lawson worked out what a fusion plasma must achieve to give out more energy than it loses. He showed that the product of plasma density and energy confinement time must exceed a minimum value at the right temperature. His report of December 1955 was secret and was published in 1957. Researchers still measure their progress against this target.

biography.name: John D. Lawson
biography.text: John David Lawson was a British engineer and physicist who worked at the Atomic Energy Research Establishment at Harwell, mainly on particle accelerators. In 1955 he wrote a short report that set out the conditions a fusion reactor must meet to produce net energy. Published in 1957, it became known as the Lawson criterion. Today the related 'triple product' of density, temperature and confinement time is the standard scorecard for every fusion experiment.

events.title: Kurchatov's lecture at Harwell
events.text: Visiting Britain, Igor Kurchatov gave a lecture at Harwell on producing thermonuclear reactions in a gas discharge. He openly described secret Soviet fusion experiments and their problems. Western scientists were surprised by both the quality and the openness. The talk was an early sign that fusion would be hard for everyone and could gain from cooperation.

biography.name: Igor Kurchatov
biography.text: Igor Kurchatov was a Soviet physicist who led the Soviet atomic bomb project; the first Soviet test took place in 1949. He then directed the hydrogen bomb work and supported research on controlled fusion at his Moscow laboratory. In the 1950s he argued for scientific exchange with the West and spoke openly about fusion in Britain in 1956. After his death the institute was renamed the Kurchatov Institute, the home of the first tokamaks.

events.title: ZETA starts up
events.text: In mid-August 1957, the large pinch machine ZETA began running at Harwell. Within weeks, deuterium shots produced about a million neutrons each, and many hoped this meant fusion. The results leaked to the press. ZETA was the biggest fusion device of its time, and Britain felt it might be ahead in the race for controlled fusion.

events.title: ZETA's headline claim
events.text: John Cockcroft held a press conference on ZETA, and full results appeared in Nature the next day, together with American papers. The British and American results were released together. Newspapers presented ZETA as a big breakthrough, but Lev Artsimovich and Lyman Spitzer were sceptical. The excitement showed how much the public wanted fusion to succeed quickly.

events.title: ZETA's neutrons were not fusion
events.text: Basil Rose's measurements showed that ZETA's neutrons flew mainly in one direction, which changed when the current was reversed. True fusion would send neutrons in all directions. The neutrons came from ions accelerated by plasma instabilities. Cockcroft published a retraction. The lesson was painful but useful: instabilities, not only temperature, decide whether a plasma can produce fusion.

events.title: Fusion research declassified in Geneva
events.text: From 1 to 13 September 1958, the second UN conference on the peaceful uses of atomic energy met in Geneva. The United States, the Soviet Union and Britain declassified their fusion research and presented it in detail. Scientists discovered that all sides faced the same unstable, leaky plasmas. From then on, fusion became one of the most open fields of science.

sources.title: Proceedings of the 2nd UN International Conference on the Peaceful Uses of Atomic Energy (UN Digital Library)
Fusion Power Associates: 1958 Geneva conference anniversary

events.title: T-1, the first tokamak
events.text: At the end of 1958, the T-1 machine began operating at Kurchatov's institute in Moscow. It is usually called the first true tokamak. Its plasma lost a lot of energy as radiation, because impurities came out of the vacuum chamber walls. Keeping the plasma clean is still a major problem in tokamaks today.

events.title: The Bohm problem
events.text: At an IAEA conference at Culham in 1965, most fusion designs were losing plasma far too fast, at a rate known as Bohm diffusion. If this was a law of nature, a fusion reactor would be impossible. Artsimovich reported Soviet tokamak results about ten times better than the Bohm limit, but many Western researchers did not believe them.

events.title: Surprise results at Novosibirsk
events.text: At the IAEA conference in Novosibirsk, 1–7 August 1968, Lev Artsimovich presented results from the T-3 tokamak: electron temperatures of about 1000 eV and confinement at least 50 times better than the Bohm limit. Many Western scientists suspected faulty measurements. Artsimovich also warned that new heating methods would be needed to go further.

biography.name: Lev Artsimovich
biography.text: Lev Artsimovich was a Soviet physicist from Moscow who led the Soviet controlled fusion programme from 1951 until his death. Often called the father of the tokamak, he presented the T-3 results that changed fusion research worldwide. He invited British scientists to check his measurements, a bold step in the Cold War. When asked when fusion power would arrive, he answered that it would come when humanity needs it, perhaps a little before.

events.title: The Culham Five confirm T-3
events.text: A British team from Culham, led by Nicol Peacock, took a laser to Moscow and measured T-3's electrons by Thomson scattering. After Derek Robinson's group made the laser much more powerful, the signal was clear: around ten million degrees, as the Soviets had claimed. Their joint paper with Soviet colleagues in Nature in November 1969 set off a worldwide 'tokamak stampede'.

sources.title: Measurement of the Electron Temperature by Thomson Scattering in Tokamak T3 (Nature, 1969; NASA ADS)

events.title: Princeton turns a stellarator into a tokamak
events.text: Persuaded by the T-3 results, Princeton converted its Model C stellarator into the Symmetric Tokamak. It closed in December 1969 and restarted in May 1970. By 1971 it had confirmed and then improved on the Soviet results. The stellarator was put aside for decades, and tokamaks became the main road to fusion.

events.title: The oil crisis boosts fusion
events.text: The Arab oil embargo of October 1973 to March 1974 made many countries worry about energy security. The United States sharply increased spending on alternative energy. Its fusion budget grew from about 40 million dollars in 1973 to 332 million in 1978. Large new machines like TFTR became possible, but expectations of quick results also grew.

sources.title: Fusion Power Associates: history of US fusion funding

events.title: PLT begins operation
events.text: The Princeton Large Torus was declared operational. To heat its plasma beyond what the current alone could do, the team added neutral beam injection: beams of fast neutral atoms shot into the plasma. Early tests heated poorly because metal impurities radiated the energy away, so the team replaced the aluminium limiter with graphite.

events.title: Europe builds JET
events.text: Culham in England was chosen as the host site on 25 October 1977, and on 30 May 1978 the European Council decided to set up the JET Joint Undertaking, which started work on 1 June 1978. JET was designed to reach conditions close to those of a reactor and to use real deuterium–tritium fuel. It showed that only international teams could afford the next step.

sources.title: Council Decision 78/471/Euratom of 30 May 1978 on the Joint European Torus (JET) Joint Undertaking (EUR-Lex)

events.title: INTOR, the first world tokamak idea
events.text: Under the International Atomic Energy Agency, scientists from Europe, Japan, the Soviet Union and the United States began the INTOR workshop to design an international tokamak reactor. It was never built, but the studies created contacts and shared methods that were used when the ITER project started a decade later.

events.title: PLT reaches 60 million degrees
events.text: Pushing its neutral beams harder, PLT reached about 60 million degrees on the night of 24 July 1978, with no sign of a feared instability. Results were shown at a conference in Innsbruck that August. Reactor-level temperatures were now possible. The result helped protect the US fusion budget from cuts, but confinement and power balance remained unsolved.

events.title: Doublet III and shaped plasmas
events.text: General Atomics in San Diego made its first plasma in Doublet III in February 1978. The machine tested non-circular, D-shaped plasmas, which can hold higher pressure without instabilities. Upgraded and renamed DIII-D in 1986, it helped make the D shape standard for tokamaks, including ITER, and it still supports ITER research.

events.title: Discovery of the H-mode
events.text: On the ASDEX tokamak in Garching, Germany, researchers found that with strong heating the plasma could suddenly jump into a 'high-confinement mode', holding its energy about twice as well. It was an unexpected and very welcome gift of nature. ITER's design relies on H-mode, although its edge can produce bursts that damage the wall.

events.title: TFTR starts in Princeton
events.text: The Tokamak Fusion Test Reactor at the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory began operating in 1982. It had been approved in the mid-1970s, during the energy crisis, and construction began in 1980. TFTR was designed to work with deuterium–tritium fuel. Handling radioactive tritium safely became a new engineering challenge that fusion research had to learn.

events.title: JET's first plasma
events.text: The Joint European Torus produced its first plasma at Culham, and Queen Elizabeth II opened it officially in April 1984. For forty years it was the largest operating tokamak and the main testing ground for ITER's physics and technology.

events.title: Japan's JT-60
events.text: Japan's large tokamak JT-60 began operating at Naka. Its first results were below predictions, which was common for new machines. After an upgrade to JT-60U in 1991, it reached very high ion temperatures and, in 1996 and 1998, conditions that would have meant break-even with deuterium–tritium fuel. With JET and TFTR, it was one of the 'big three' tokamaks.

events.title: Reagan and Gorbachev in Geneva
events.text: At their first summit, held in Geneva from 19 to 21 November 1985, Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev proposed to US President Ronald Reagan that their countries build a fusion experiment together. The Cold War rivals were looking for ways to cooperate. This idea grew into ITER, with Europe and Japan as partners too.

events.title: ITER gets its name
events.text: After the 1986 Reykjavik summit created a committee for the project, an IAEA meeting in Vienna in March 1987 launched conceptual design studies. The machine was named ITER, the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor; 'iter' is also Latin for 'the way'. The four partners were the European Community, Japan, the Soviet Union and the United States.

events.title: ITER's conceptual design
events.text: From 1988 to 1990, international teams worked out ITER's conceptual design, and the engineering design followed from 1992 to 1998. Designing a machine that had never existed, with parts made in many countries, took years. A detailed design was finally confirmed in 2001. This slow start is part of why ITER is still not finished.

events.title: The cold fusion affair
events.text: Chemists Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons announced at a press conference in Utah that they had produced fusion at room temperature in a small electrochemical cell. Laboratories around the world tried to repeat it and failed. Like Huemul and ZETA, cold fusion showed the danger of announcing results before other scientists can check them.

events.title: JET's first deuterium–tritium fusion
events.text: JET carried out the first experiments with a deuterium–tritium mixture in a magnetic fusion device. Fuel containing tritium produces far more fusion energy than deuterium alone, but it is radioactive and makes the machine itself radioactive. This first step proved that real reactor fuel could be handled safely in a large tokamak.

events.title: ASDEX Upgrade starts
events.text: The ASDEX Upgrade tokamak began operating in Garching. It was built to study the plasma edge and divertor, the part where exhaust heat and particles leave the plasma. Later it was lined with tungsten, the metal chosen for ITER's hottest surfaces. Handling such heat loads is one of the hardest engineering problems of a fusion power plant.

events.title: TFTR burns 50–50 fuel
events.text: In December 1993, TFTR began serious experiments with an equal mix of deuterium and tritium, the fuel planned for future power plants. In 1994 it produced a then world record of 10.7 megawatts of fusion power, and in 1995 it reached 510 million degrees. TFTR was shut down in 1997, before any successor was built in the United States.

events.title: JT-60U and 'equivalent' break-even
events.text: Japan's JT-60U reported an equivalent gain of 1.05, meaning that its plasma would have produced slightly more fusion power than the heating power if it had used deuterium–tritium fuel. In 1998 the value rose to 1.25. The machine only used deuterium, so these were estimates. It showed how carefully fusion records must be read.

events.title: JET's 16 megawatt record
events.text: In 1997, JET produced 16 megawatts of fusion power from 24 megawatts of heating, a gain of about 0.67, and 22 megajoules of fusion energy in one pulse. JET itself broke the energy record only in 2021. The alpha particles from fusion also heated the plasma measurably. Yet the gain was still below one, and the peak lasted less than a second.

events.title: Tore Supra's six-minute plasma
events.text: In December 2003, the French tokamak Tore Supra at Cadarache held a plasma for about six and a half minutes, with over a gigajoule of injected energy. Long pulses are needed for a power plant, but they create constant heat loads on the wall. Tore Supra was later rebuilt as WEST with tungsten parts to test ITER technology.

events.title: Cadarache chosen for ITER
events.text: After a long contest between sites in France and Japan, the ITER partners agreed at a meeting in Moscow to build the machine at Cadarache in southern France. Japan received a compensating role, including extra research projects. Choosing a site took about two years and showed how political interests can slow a scientific project.

events.title: China's EAST
events.text: China's Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokamak in Hefei made its first plasma. It was the first tokamak with all its main magnets superconducting. Superconducting coils use little power, so they allow very long pulses. EAST quickly became a leader in long-duration operation, part of China's rapidly growing fusion programme.

events.title: The ITER Agreement
events.text: At the Élysée Palace in Paris, ministers of seven partners signed the ITER Agreement: China, the European Union, India, Japan, Russia, South Korea and the United States. Each member contributes money, people and machine parts. Sharing the work spreads the cost, but it also means that decisions and deliveries must be coordinated between many governments.

events.title: The ITER Organization is born
events.text: After all partners had ratified the agreement, the ITER Organization was officially established. Site clearing at Cadarache had started in March 2007. The first cost estimate was about 5 to 6 billion euros; later estimates are several times higher. Rising costs and delays became one of the central stories of the project.

events.title: South Korea's KSTAR
events.text: The Korea Superconducting Tokamak Advanced Research device produced its first plasma in Daejeon in 2008. Like EAST, it uses superconducting magnets. KSTAR later specialised in holding plasmas hotter than 100 million degrees for many seconds. Such long, hot pulses are needed to show that a tokamak can run steadily, not just in short bursts.

events.title: NIF completed
events.text: The National Ignition Facility at Lawrence Livermore in California was certified complete, years late and well over budget. Its 192 lasers squeeze a tiny fuel capsule so hard that it fuses for a very short moment. The first ignition campaign, until 2012, failed. NIF also serves nuclear weapons research, which is a main reason for its funding.

events.title: EUROfusion founded
events.text: European fusion laboratories signed an agreement creating the EUROfusion consortium to coordinate their research. It follows a joint European roadmap aimed at ITER and then a demonstration power plant called DEMO. Combining national programmes reduces duplication, but it also means decisions depend on many governments and budgets.

events.title: Wendelstein 7-X starts
events.text: The Wendelstein 7-X stellarator in Greifswald, Germany, produced its first plasma, using helium; the first hydrogen plasma followed on 3 February 2016. Its twisted magnet coils were designed by supercomputer to avoid the problems of early stellarators. Stellarators do not need a large plasma current, so they may run steadily without some of the tokamak's instabilities.

events.title: WEST, a testbed for ITER
events.text: After an upgrade from 2013 to 2016, the old Tore Supra tokamak restarted in December 2016 as WEST. Its new tungsten divertor is used to test the same kind of components that ITER will need. Testing such parts under real plasma conditions is essential, because a damaged divertor could stop a power plant for months.

events.title: W7-X sets a stellarator record
events.text: In June 2018, Wendelstein 7-X reached a record fusion triple product for a stellarator, with ion temperatures near 40 million degrees. This was a sign that the computer-optimised design really worked. It brought the stellarator back as a serious alternative to the tokamak, almost fifty years after Princeton gave it up.

events.title: ITER machine assembly begins
events.text: After the 1,250-tonne base of the cryostat was installed in May 2020, ITER formally launched assembly of the tokamak itself. ITER is designed to produce about 500 megawatts of fusion power from 50 megawatts of heating, a gain of ten. Putting together millions of parts from many countries is a huge engineering task.

events.title: MAST Upgrade starts
events.text: The MAST Upgrade spherical tokamak began operating at Culham. A spherical tokamak is compact, shaped more like a cored apple than a doughnut. MAST-U tests the Super-X divertor, which is meant to cut the heat load on the wall about tenfold. Its results feed into STEP, a planned British prototype power plant for the 2040s.

events.title: A 20-tesla superconducting magnet
events.text: In September 2021, Commonwealth Fusion Systems and MIT tested a large high-temperature superconducting magnet that reached 20 tesla, a record for such magnets. Stronger fields allow much smaller tokamaks. The company began building its SPARC tokamak in Devens, Massachusetts, the same year. Private companies are now a growing part of fusion research.

events.title: EAST runs for over 1,000 seconds
events.text: Earlier in 2021, EAST had held 120 million degrees for 101 seconds. On 30 December it sustained a high-performance plasma for 1,056 seconds, about 17 and a half minutes. Long pulses test whether walls, cooling systems and control can work continuously. A power plant would have to run for hours or days, not minutes.

events.title: JET produces 59 megajoules
events.text: In a new deuterium–tritium campaign, JET produced 59 megajoules of fusion energy in a pulse lasting five seconds, more than double its 1997 energy record. The experiment was designed to test plasma conditions and wall materials planned for ITER. Even so, the plasma still needed more heating power than it produced.

events.title: Ignition at NIF
events.text: NIF's lasers delivered 2.05 megajoules to a fuel target, and the target released 3.15 megajoules of fusion energy, a target gain of about 1.5. It was the first time a fusion experiment produced more energy than was put into the fuel. But making the laser pulse took about 300 megajoules from the grid, so the facility as a whole used far more energy than it made.

events.title: EAST holds H-mode for 403 seconds
events.text: EAST kept a plasma in high-confinement mode for 403 seconds, a record for this mode. H-mode is the operating state planned for ITER, but it is harder to keep stable for long times. Running a high-performance plasma for many minutes is an important step towards steady operation in a fusion power plant.

events.title: JT-60SA's first plasma
events.text: The superconducting tokamak JT-60SA, built by Japan and Europe at Naka, produced its first plasma and was inaugurated on 1 December 2023. It is the largest operating superconducting tokamak. Commissioning had been delayed by a short circuit in 2021 that needed long repairs, a reminder of how fragile complex magnet systems can be.

events.title: JET's final energy record
events.text: In October 2023, in its last deuterium–tritium experiments, JET produced 69 megajoules of fusion energy over about six seconds from only 0.21 milligrams of fuel. The record was announced in February 2024. The tiny fuel mass shows fusion's huge energy density, but JET still needed much more heating energy than its plasma produced.

events.title: JET's last plasma
events.text: In December 2023, after about 40 years and more than 105,000 pulses, JET ended operations. Its decommissioning is itself an experiment: engineers study how a tritium-using machine is taken apart and how its radioactive parts are handled. JET's long life shows how many years each step in fusion research takes.

events.title: KSTAR's 48 seconds at 100 million degrees
events.text: The Korean institute announced that KSTAR had kept ions above 100 million degrees for 48 seconds and had held H-mode for 102 seconds, during a campaign from December 2023 to February 2024. New tungsten divertor parts handled the heat better than the old carbon ones. Hot plasmas and durable walls must work together in a reactor.

sources.title: Green light on continuous fusion plasma operations technology (EurekAlert!)

events.title: ITER's new schedule
events.text: ITER presented a new baseline plan. Research operation is now planned to start in 2034, deuterium–deuterium plasmas in 2035 and deuterium–tritium operation in 2039. The earlier first-plasma goal of 2025 was abandoned after defects were found in key components; repairs and changes were estimated to cost about 5 billion euros extra.

events.title: EAST's 1,066-second record
events.text: EAST sustained a plasma for 1,066 seconds, beating its own 2021 record of 1,056 seconds. Records like this are not about producing energy: EAST uses deuterium only. They test whether superconducting magnets, heating systems and cooled walls can run together for a long time, which ITER and later power plants will need.

events.title: WEST's 22-minute plasma
events.text: The WEST tokamak at Cadarache kept a plasma going for 1,337 seconds, more than 22 minutes, a new record for pulse length. It ran at lower temperatures than a reactor would, but its tungsten walls and cooling systems coped with the long heat load. Such tests show whether ITER-type components survive real conditions.

events.title: NIF's 8.6 megajoule shot
events.text: NIF delivered 2.08 megajoules of laser energy to a target and got about 8.6 megajoules of fusion energy back, a record target gain of 4.13. Since 2022, NIF has repeated ignition several times. Still, a laser fusion power plant would need much more efficient lasers and many shots every second, with cheap targets.

events.title: First vacuum vessel module in ITER's pit
events.text: The first of nine large vacuum vessel sector modules was lowered into the ITER tokamak pit, after repairs to welding defects found earlier. These modules together form the steel chamber that will hold the plasma. Assembly had been stopped for about two years because of the defects, which shows how one manufacturing problem can delay a whole project.

events.title: Wendelstein 7-X's long-pulse record
events.text: During its campaign from February to May 2025, Wendelstein 7-X set a world record for the triple product in a long plasma, and ran a discharge of about six minutes with 1.8 gigajoules of energy turnover. Combining good confinement with long duration is exactly what a power plant needs, and stellarators are now taken seriously again.

events.title: SPARC's first big magnet
events.text: In January 2026, Commonwealth Fusion Systems completed the first of SPARC's 18 toroidal field magnets and placed it on an assembly jig. The company plans first plasma around 2027 and hopes to reach a gain above one, with an expected gain of about 11. These are plans, not results; earlier dates for SPARC have already slipped.

events.title: ITER's central solenoid completed
events.text: The sixth and final module of ITER's central solenoid was stacked at Cadarache. This tall superconducting magnet in the centre of the machine drives the electric current in the plasma. Completing the stack, nearly two decades after the ITER Agreement, shows both the progress and the slow pace of the project.

events.title: Two-thirds of ITER's core in place
events.text: With the sixth of nine vacuum vessel modules lowered into the pit, ITER reported that about two-thirds of the tokamak core was in place, nearly six months ahead of its new schedule. The last module is expected in 2027. After many years of delays, assembly is now advancing steadily, but deuterium–tritium operation is still planned only for 2039.
